scenes.title: Cold open
narration: The Cat Who Became a King
This is Malaysian Lion Dance. Tang dynasty to present.
on_screen: Title card: Malaysian Lion Dance · Malaysia · Tang dynasty to present

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The lion is not native to China; the dance likely originated in Persia or India and reached China via Central Asia during the Han dynasty.

Detailed descriptions appeared in the Tang dynasty, where it was known as 'Great Peace Music.' The Southern Lion style, which prevails in Malaysia, developed later in Guangdong, possibly during the Ming dynasty, as an adaptation of Northern styles to local myths like the Nian monster.
It was brought to Southeast Asia by the Southern Chinese diaspora.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: It is performed during 'Lunar New Year and other traditional, cultural and religious festivals' to 'bring good luck and fortune and to ward off evil.' It is a staple of business openings and weddings.

The dance is a 'ceremony to exorcise spirits' and is often performed to 'honor special guests.' In a village setting, the lion pays respects to the local temple and ancestors before dancing through the streets.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance is performed by two people: one manipulates the head and the other the tail.
It involves 'kung fu moves and postures' to maintain stances.

The Hok San style specifically mimics the 'natural movements of a real animal—particularly a cat.' Performers use a 'martial style' for acrobatics and a 'civil style' for character-driven movements like blinking and ear-twitching.
Watch for Choy Chang, Jong jumping.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Performances are accompanied by a 'vigorous drumbeat with gongs and cymbals.' The primary instrument is the 'chinesischen Fasstrommel Shigu' (lion drum).
In the Hok San style, specific drum patterns are synchronized with the lion's movements to enhance the feline quality of the dance.
Listen for the Shigu (lion drum), Gongs, Cymbals.
The pulse is 4/4 or irregular based on movement at about 120 beats a minute.
A loud, percussive wall of sound dominated by a large barrel drum, punctuated by the metallic crash of cymbals and gongs that mirror the lion's every blink and pounce.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: The Southern Lion has a 'single horn' and a head made of papier-mâché over bamboo or aluminum.
It features 'pop-up teeth, tongue, and eyes that swivel.' The body is made of layered cloth trimmed with fur.
Colors are symbolic: yellow for Liu Bei (wisdom), red for Guan Gong (courage), and black for Zhang Fei (aggression).

scenes.title: The people
narration: Feng Gengzhang (馮庚長) is the founder of the Hok San style, which is highly popular in Malaysia.

Li Yi Sheng (李怡生), a disciple of Feng, introduced the Hok San style to Singapore and Malaysia in the 1920s, founding the Singapore Hok San Association Lion Dance Troupe which influenced the wider region.
The two main types are Northern and Southern.
The dance is a subclass of Chinese dance and is closely linked to Chinese martial arts.

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: Malaysian Lion Dance is parent of Kung Fu: Lion dance movements are fundamentally derived from Chinese martial arts stances.
Malaysian Lion Dance is sibling of Shishi-mai: The Japanese variant of the lion dance, also used for New Year luck.

scenes.title: A respectful note
narration: The dance is a ritual for exorcising evil spirits and honoring deities; performers often pay respects at temples before beginning.
